title: Getting Projects Creatively Under Way: The Five Phases of Project Planning
coreMove: Move a project from vague intention through purpose, outcome, raw ideas, structure, and one next physical action.
sourcePressure: The chapter teaches natural project planning through purpose and principles, outcome visioning, brainstorming, organizing, and next actions, with a simple dining-out example as supported illustration.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Turning planning into a polished project plan before the purpose, desired outcome, and next move are clear.
sourceAnchorNote: The source sidecar contains no chapter-specific named people, named studies, or named places. Use only the listed GTD terms, official metadata, or supported artifacts; do not invent anecdotes.

sourceAnchors.name: dining-out example
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar supports a simple dining-out example that demonstrates purpose, standards, desired result, brainstorming, organizing, and next action.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Even choosing dinner has a natural plan: why go, what counts as good, what options exist, how to choose, and who makes the reservation.

sourceAnchors.name: five phases of natural project planning
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar names purpose and principles, outcome visioning, brainstorming, organizing, and next actions.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Natural planning expands before it narrows, then it earns closure with a visible next action.

hook: stress is not about having too much to do
a messy desk proves the system is broken
counterintuition: the real problem is not time but attention
this is not about doing more but doing what matters
the simple move is actually the powerful one
tryThisNow: set a timer and write everything down
pick one task and make it specific
review your list and choose a priority
examples: timestamp plus name plus laptop plus decision repeated across all six examples
home kitchen clutter as mental-load shorthand

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person 'You' direct address, retrospective 'It took her three weeks to see', question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.domain: a community theater lighting plot two weeks before rehearsal
exampleSpecs.audience: a volunteer director moving from enthusiasm to usable production work
exampleSpecs.stakes: opening rehearsal may burn two hours if lighting needs stay vague
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The empty stage is still dark when Claire writes why the first rehearsal matters before touching the lighting spreadsheet.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: an unlit stage with tape marks on the floor

exampleSpecs.domain: a dental clinic planning its first Saturday pediatric day
exampleSpecs.audience: a clinic manager balancing service quality and staff limits
exampleSpecs.stakes: families could arrive to a kind idea with no workable flow
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: "What would a good Saturday look like at 10:30?" Daniel asks before the team starts listing supplies.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a pediatric toothbrush sample beside a blank schedule grid
mustAvoid: drifting into persuasion or health education

exampleSpecs.domain: a neighborhood mutual-aid group designing winter coat pickup
exampleSpecs.audience: a coordinator who needs logistics without killing volunteer energy
exampleSpecs.stakes: donated coats may pile up without sizes, pickup flow, or storage rules
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Plastic garment bags rustle as Chloe lets every idea hit the wall before anyone argues about feasibility.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: plastic garment bags on a church basement table
mustAvoid: making brainstorming sound like corporate ideation

exampleSpecs.domain: a software security team planning a password reset after a vendor breach
exampleSpecs.audience: a technical lead who must move fast without skipping standards
exampleSpecs.stakes: a rushed reset could lock out customers or leave exposed accounts open
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: What happens if Henrik starts with tasks instead of first naming the successful end state and non-negotiable security principles?
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a breach notification printed beside a laptop

exampleSpecs.domain: a city parks crew preparing a one-day playground repair
exampleSpecs.audience: a supervisor coordinating permits, parts, and public notices
exampleSpecs.stakes: children could return Monday to a fenced-off structure because no next action was owned
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At 7:35 a.m., Yusuf turns "fix playground" into outcome, loose parts list, workstreams, and the first call to the parts supplier.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a locked playground gate with orange mesh
mustAvoid: making it just about task breakdown

exampleSpecs.domain: a podcast producer launching a limited interview series for a museum
exampleSpecs.audience: a producer balancing creative promise with release deadlines
exampleSpecs.stakes: recording dates could drift while the concept keeps sounding exciting
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: It took Giulia three enthusiastic planning calls to notice that nobody had named the finished show or the next booking email.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a microphone case open beside a museum floor plan

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

skillTargets: turn a brainstorm into organized next action

tryThisNowSpec: For one stalled project, write why it matters, one sentence for done, three raw ideas, one grouping, and the next physical action.
